pr_body:
This creates a new more logic backend manager that handles all backend operations.

For each top-level operation, there is now a single backend manager instance that is passed to sub-commands.

The internals of the backend manager are now rewritten to use async logic instead of threading.

The design uses a single task runner that dispatches operations and honors concurrent settings and limits from one place.

The logic for each operation has been moved into a separate files/classes to make it easier to understand each operation.

This fixes #5804

issue_context.title: Rewrite the BackendManager and BackendUploader
issue_context.body:
The BackendManager was written before channel based communication was used.
This results in a overwhelming interface with many variables shared across functionality and quite a few locks and signals.
At the same time, the BackendUploader has copied some of the code to support parallel uploads.

The two classes should be rewritten into a single abstraction for the backends that supports features from both.
comments: I'm curious if this has any bearing on the backend separate process that's sometimes mentioned in the forum and Issues.

This issue has been mentioned on **Duplicati**. There might be relevant details there:

https://forum.duplicati.com/t/ftp-without-ssl-fails-with-2-1-0-2-beta-2024-11-29/19691/40

> I'm curious if this has any bearing on the backend separate process that's sometimes mentioned in the forum and Issues.

I do not intend to include that in the fix here. It requires some inter-process communication to get a separate backend process running, and we don't have a great foundation for that yet.

For this issue, I plan to rewrite it so everything related to backend communication is abstracted away inside the BackendManager, and that can then use channels to delegate work. Once we get IPC ready, it should be trivial to boot up individual processes and delegate work to them.

review_comments: Shouldn't it have similar fields, such as this one, for downloads?

The logic here is to cache the option values explicitly.

There is no limit to parallel downloads because downloads are always done one at a time.
It is possible to download in parallel, but the calling code becomes complex when dealing with pending transfers, once error handling is added.
For that reason, there is only overlapping download, where the processing is done while downloading the next file.

Shouldn't this have a try/catch?
No. The logic here is that the execution does not catch errors. Errors are propagated to the handler, which will deal with retry logic etc.

Shouldn't get operations be queue-able as well?

The reason that GET operations are not queued is that they have a return value. If one or more operations fail, something needs to deal with in-flight GET requests.
In the current code, there is only overlapping download.

For large backups (or at least a large number of volumes) I think this will be quite time consuming. If this ever becomes a problem, it should be batched (reducing the number of calls to list and the number of traversals of the list), or maybe the backend support supplying a filter?

Yes, this will be slow for large remote lists. The list operation itself is slow, and iterating it is also slow.
The option is default off, so it has minimal impact. It was initially introduced to guard against issues where the backend would fail to store the file properly.

Since we only iterate the list once, and the content is expected to be new on each call, I don't see a good way to make it faster.
Addressed in issue #5917
Why are unencrypted files not being tracked?

This is a special "feature" where you can upload a JSON file with the size and hashes of each file.
There is a Python script you can run on the remote destination to verify the contents (`--upload-verification-file`).
This file needs to not be encrypted, so the remote destination can verify that all files exist and are pristine, without knowing the encryption passphrase.

## Hard-coded credentials

The hard-coded value "recreated-database.sqlite" flows to [access to local variable username](1) which is compared against [access to field Username](2).

[Show more details](https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/security/code-scanning/189)

For very _very_ large backups, won't this string become very large, thus producing a giant memory footprint and explode in the log?

Yes it will. It has been this way for a long time, but I also noticed it during the rewrite.
The idea is to record the actual list results in the database for debugging purposes.

Only thing I can think of to improve it would be to have an actual table with the list results, so it does not need to be in memory. But this is a bit hard to achieve, because the database may be used elsewhere during the list operation.
And, the debugging feature is not a "must have".

If you have ideas for how to improve it, lets discuss.
